name: Uma Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the extrusion press at Northgate Extrusions. We push hot aluminium through a steel die, like squeezing toothpaste, and out comes a long profile for window frames, forty metres of it at a time. I watch the temperature and speed, change the dies, cut the profiles with the hot saw and check them against the drawing. There's already a robot stacker at the end, so I'm half operator, half babysitter for it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing a problem with numbers. Last year I got fed up with nobody knowing why we scrapped so much, so I built a spreadsheet with an AI tool to track it, and now the supervisor uses it every morning. I use AI every day, for that and for reading the press manuals. What wears me out is the heat by the press in summer, and my partner Arjun's a postman, so he's up at four and I'm up at five and the kids get a tired version of both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. It's good at some things and bad at others, like any tool. I'd probably say I'm still using it for the spreadsheets, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a bit disappointed, but fine. My job stays, and I keep the little edge I've got from being the person who knows the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep improving the scrap tracker, maybe ask for a small pay bump for it, because it's saved them money. Savings stay where they are, about four months. Tara wants a laptop for school, we'd get her that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, mostly. A bit bored by the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a pay bump. Have you asked before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I've got the numbers, we cut scrap from six percent to just over four. I've been waiting for the right month. Maybe after the annual stock count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot stacker came in three years ago and two stacking jobs went. That would carry on, AI or no AI. I just make sure I'm the one who knows how to restart it when it jams.

S0.say: I'm not surprised: it's good at some things and bad at others, like any tool. I'd say I'm still using it for the spreadsheets, because I would be.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, but fine. My job stays and I keep the small edge of being the person who knows the tools.
S0.do: Keeps improving her scrap tracker and plans to ask for a pay rise after the annual stock count, using the drop in scrap from six to four percent. Keeps four months saved and buys Tara a school laptop.
S0.feel: Calm and mostly pleased, if a little bored.
S0.quote: I just make sure I'm the one who knows how to restart it when it jams.
S0.fieldNote: Uma has already made herself useful with AI and has numbers to prove it. Her approach to the robot stacker, being the one who restarts it, sums up her strategy. She hasn't yet cashed in on her value, which is a small gap between confidence and action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be smart about it. The people who learn the new kit will be fine, and the company should help the others learn it. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I'm already the one on the line who uses this stuff. If the saw gets a camera and the press gets AI that sets the speed, someone has to run it, and I'd make sure that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the plant manager in the first month with a plan for a robot on the saw, written up with AI help, costs and payback. I'd ask to be the one trained on it by the supplier. I'd keep learning the AI tools, maybe one of the free courses on factory automation online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit buzzy, like before a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd propose a robot that might take someone's job. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit uncomfortable. But if I don't, the supplier's salesman will, and then it's put in by someone who doesn't know our line. Better me than him. I'd ask that the saw lad moves to quality, not out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager says no, or gives it to someone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask the supplier if they're hiring. They always need people who know a real line, not just the brochure. I'm not going to sit and sulk.

S1.say: It's happening, so let's be smart about it. People who learn the new kit will be fine, and the company should help the others learn it.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, because I'm already the one on the line who uses this stuff. If the saw gets a camera and the press gets AI that sets the speed, someone has to run it, and I'd make sure that's me.
S1.do: Pitches a robot on the saw to the plant manager in the first month, with costs and payback written up using AI. Asks to be trained by the supplier, takes free online automation courses, and approaches the supplier for work if she's passed over.
S1.feel: Calm and a little buzzy, like before a new job.
S1.quote: If I don't, the supplier's salesman will, and then it's put in by someone who doesn't know our line.
S1.fieldNote: Uma would bring automation in herself, reasoning that it's coming anyway and she knows the line best. She's uncomfortable about the saw operator and tries to protect him with a move to quality. Her fallback, joining the supplier, shows she isn't tied to Northgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and companies and the government need to work out quickly how people pay their bills. I wouldn't be shouting about it, I'd be practical. Like, here's what we need, here's what it costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years scares me. Being good with the tools only helps if there's a gap between what the tools can do and what I can do. With full AGI and robots, there's no gap. I'm one step ahead of a train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd move fast. Get savings up from four months to six by cutting the summer holiday and the second car. I'd go straight to the robot supplier for a commissioning job, because for a couple of years they'll need people to install all this. And I'd put a small slice of savings into a fund that holds the robot and AI companies. If they're going to win, I want a tiny piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Clear-headed, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying shares a risk when your cushion's only a few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's why it'd be small, maybe a month's worth, not the whole lot. Arjun would argue with me. He'd want it all in the bank. We'd meet somewhere in the middle, we usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One job move, maybe two. Installing robots in other people's factories until there are no factories left needing it. It buys the kids a couple of years of normal, which matters. It doesn't buy a career.

S2.say: It's too fast, and companies and government need to work out quickly how people will pay their bills. I'd be practical, not shouting: here's what we need and what it costs.
S2.think: Two years scares me, because being good with the tools only helps while there's a gap between what they can do and what I can do. With full AGI and robots there's no gap, and I'm one step ahead of a train.
S2.do: Cuts the summer holiday and second car to lift savings from four to six months. Goes straight to the robot supplier for a commissioning job and puts about a month's savings into a fund holding AI and robot companies.
S2.quote: With full AGI and robots, there's no gap. I'm one step ahead of a train.
S2.fieldNote: Uma knows her edge depends on a gap between her and the machines, and AGI closes it. She moves fast and even bets a little on the robot makers, while keeping it small because of her partner. She values the two years mainly as time for her kids to have a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now. Train people, plan, and stop pretending it's not coming. I'd probably put a post up about it, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a decent run for me. I could get properly qualified in automation, get a few years of good money installing and setting up robots, and save hard. It's not forever, but it's a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up this year for a part-time automation certificate at the college, the one that covers robot programming, about a year of evenings. I'd move to the supplier or a robot installer by year two. Save harder, aim for a year of expenses by the end. And put a bit into that fund each month, not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in charge. Like I'm driving, not a passenger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A year of savings is a big jump from four months. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Installer money's better than press money, maybe twenty percent. If we live on the old wage and save the difference, plus no holidays abroad, we'd get there by year five. Tight, but it's arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the people on your line who aren't like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That bothers me. Tony on nights hates computers. I'd try to get him on a course, but you can't drag a grown man. I'd feel bad leaving, a bit like leaving a party early when you know it's about to get messy.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if we start now: train people, plan, and stop pretending it's not coming. I'd put a post up about it, nothing dramatic.
S3.think: Five years is a decent run for me. I could get qualified in automation, earn good money installing robots for a few years and save hard, which is a bridge if not forever.
S3.do: Starts a year-long evening automation certificate this year and moves to a robot supplier or installer by year two. Lives on her old wage to bank the extra pay, aiming for a year of expenses by year five, and adds a little to the fund monthly.
S3.feel: Uneasy but in charge, like driving rather than being a passenger.
S3.quote: I'd feel bad leaving, a bit like leaving a party early when you know it's about to get messy.
S3.fieldNote: Uma treats five years as a bridge and has the arithmetic worked out. Her plan is personal, not political; she wants planning, not protest. Her unease shows mainly when she thinks of colleagues like Tony who won't follow her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who doesn't use it is choosing not to. That sounds harsh, so maybe I'd say it nicer at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough for me to do well before it ends. Five years installing, then maybe running a team of installers. By the end I'd be fifty-three with savings and some shares, and the kids grown. After that I honestly don't know what anyone does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same start as the five-year one: the certificate, then the move. Then I'd keep building. Push savings past a year, keep adding to the fund, maybe help Tara pick a degree that works with machines instead of against them. I'd go slower on the risky stuff, because there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end, but mostly I'd feel lucky. Lucky I like this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'after that I don't know what anyone does'. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than I let on. I'm good at being useful. If nobody needs anybody to be useful, I don't know who I am on a Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who don't use the time are choosing not to. Is that fair to someone like Tony?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. He's got a bad back and his wife's ill. Choosing isn't the same for everyone. I'll take that back a bit.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and anyone who doesn't use it is choosing not to. That sounds harsh, so maybe I'd say it nicer at work.
S4.think: Ten years is enough for me to do well before it ends, installing and then running a team. After that, at fifty-three, I honestly don't know what anyone does.
S4.do: Takes the automation certificate, moves to robot installation and works towards leading a team. Pushes savings past a year, keeps adding to the fund, and helps Tara choose a degree that works with machines.
S4.feel: Uneasy about where it ends, but mostly lucky to enjoy this kind of work.
S4.quote: If nobody needs anybody to be useful, I don't know who I am on a Tuesday.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Uma is confident about her own path but unsettled by what comes after, because her sense of self rests on being useful. When challenged about Tony she softened her hard line and admitted choice isn't equal. That willingness to take something back is very her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can outrun slow change, I can't outrun a train. What would help is cheap, fast training on real robots, not videos, and some kind of income guarantee for the in-between months so people like Tony aren't on their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose by not making things anymore. Every window frame in this town came through our press. My kids point at them. I don't know what they'll point at.

headlineQuote: Every window frame in this town came through our press. My kids point at them. I don't know what they'll point at.
portrait: Uma Gupta, 43, runs the extrusion press at Northgate Extrusions, making aluminium window-frame profiles, and uses AI every day, most proudly for a scrap tracker that cut waste. She's pragmatic and fast-moving: in the milder pictures she'd propose the robots herself and ask to run them. AGI in two years makes her anxious because her edge over the machines vanishes, but with five or ten years she plans an automation certificate, a move to a robot installer and steady saving. What unsettles her most is not money but who she'd be if nobody needed her to be useful.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because she can outrun slow change but can't outrun a train.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast training on real robots rather than videos, and an income guarantee for the in-between months so less adaptable colleagues aren't left alone.
